cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: The National Minimum Wage sets legal pay floors based on age: lower rates for under-18s and 18-20 year olds, a higher rate for 21-22 year olds, and the National Living Wage for workers aged 23+.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: Workers have the right to a written statement of employment terms from day one, including pay, hours, holiday entitlement, and notice periods.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: The maximum working week is 48 hours (averaged over 17 weeks) unless the worker voluntarily opts out. Young workers (under 18) are limited to 40 hours per week and 8 hours per day.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: Workers are entitled to at least 5.6 weeks (28 days for full-time) of paid holiday per year, which can include bank holidays.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 requires employers to provide a safe working environment, and employees have a duty to follow safety procedures.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: Unfair dismissal protection applies after 2 years of continuous employment (1 year in Northern Ireland). Employers must follow fair procedures and have a valid reason for dismissal.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: Trade unions represent workers' interests through collective bargaining on pay and conditions, and can organise industrial action (with a ballot) as a last resort.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: The Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination in employment on the basis of protected characteristics — in recruitment, promotion, pay, and dismissal.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: Zero-hours contracts offer no guaranteed hours of work. Workers are only paid for hours worked, creating income insecurity. They are legal but controversial.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: The gig economy (Uber, Deliveroo, etc.) has raised questions about employment status: are workers 'employees' (full rights), 'workers' (some rights), or 'self-employed' (few rights)?

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: The Supreme Court ruled in Uber v Aslam (2021) that Uber drivers are 'workers' entitled to the minimum wage and holiday pay, not self-employed contractors.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Employment Rights
cards.back: Acas (Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service) provides free advice and resolves workplace disputes before they reach employment tribunal.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — employment rights?
cards.back: 1. For Employment Rights questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Employment Rights to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate the extent to which employment law protects workers from exploitation. [12 marks]
